topic: continual learning; multimodal learning; benchmark validity; literature-mining quality
status: bounded candidate from 12-paper uniform-random topic draw, ten newly audited full texts, two existing frame audits, and two independent benchmark follow-ups; not a novelty claim or prevalence estimate
claim: The current `continual_multimodal_learning` retrieval bucket mixes distinct problems, so its records cannot be treated as one field-level evidence set. Within the directly relevant continual-learning subset, evidence across older task-pair experiments, graph/image replay benchmarks, CLiMB, and MLLM-CTBench indicates that forgetting and method outcomes depend on task order, modality, backbone, dataset, and resource protocol. A matched cross-regime test of continual-learning method-ranking portability is a defensible next experiment, but this audit does not establish that prior work has never done it.
positive_evidence: In the 2013 gradient-based forgetting study, dropout has the best old/new-task trade-off in the tested three task-pair settings, while activation-function rankings vary with task relation.
CLiMB (2022) evaluates sequential vision-language tasks and reports task-order sensitivity; common methods mitigate some forgetting but do not produce positive upstream transfer in its tested setup.
MLLM-CTBench (2025/2026 version) evaluates eight methods across seven tasks/six domains and two task orders, reporting dependence on base model strength, task sequence, and method regime.

Coreset studies show measurable gains within specified protocols, but use different datasets and constraints: the 2020 bilevel method reports five-run results on Permuted/Split MNIST and Split CIFAR-10 and notes significant overhead for summaries above 500; 2025 PDAC evaluates three image-classification continual-learning benchmarks, with three runs in streaming tables.

The twelve sampled records include direct continual-learning work alongside contest design, static multimodal representations/fusion, targeted LLM unlearning, image-generation interpretability, and active cross-modal benchmark design; this is enough to show this particular retrieval bucket is heterogeneous, though not enough to estimate corpus-wide label precision.
counterevidence: CLiMB and MLLM-CTBench already supply multimodal continual-learning benchmarks; absence of such benchmarks is not a valid gap claim.

EscapeCraft-4D addresses a narrower combination of interactive action, spatial audio, transient clues, misleading audio, and time limits not equivalent to continual-learning benchmarks; its own evidence is simulated and small, with non-identical GPT-4o API configuration.
The positive c-EB/PDAC/DiCGRL results are meaningful within their own reported datasets; heterogeneity of protocols does not imply those results are false.
A broad topic label and ten false/adjacent records in this draw do not establish the false-positive rate of the full 198,690-candidate corpus.

falsifiable_test: Choose representative regularization, replay/coreset, and architecture-based methods. On one fixed code/model suite, match training data, task orders, memory, optimizer steps, and accelerator time; evaluate at least one vision-only sequence, one graph sequence, and one vision-language/MLLM sequence with at least five seeds and both forward/reversed task orders. Report average accuracy, forgetting, new-task learning, transfer, memory, latency, and per-regime method ranks. The portability hypothesis is weakened if a method ranking remains stable across modalities, task orders, and model scales under those controls; it is strengthened if rankings reverse systematically with those factors.
limitations: This is an audit of a single 12-record random topic draw plus selected benchmark follow-ups. The draw is not large enough to estimate topic precision or literature prevalence. The sources use different model generations and tasks; no effect sizes are pooled. The proposed matched study is a candidate opportunity, not a novelty assertion.
